tells: The ASCII/character-field rendering stays consistent across very different subjects: a walking figure, a coin flying through a field of streaming glyphs, a planet with orbiting labels, padlocks, a grid of spinning coins. That range of art direction points to real production, not one effect applied to everything.
There is evidence of choreography: the coin travels on a curve through flowing glyph streams, the planet orbits, and the final grid shows coins at different rotation phases.
Monochrome International Klein-ish blue with white is a deliberate, committed palette.

Weaknesses: the idea is literal (crypto = $ signs + code + padlocks). The filler code reads machine-written ('**Direct Payment**' with markdown asterisks, 'Matching Cut Transition("circular")'), the type is a default monospace with highlight-box labels, and the ASCII-render look is a heavily trended style.
gaps: Replace the literal crypto iconography ($, padlocks, coins) with a metaphor only this brand could own; C turns 'computing' into light, heat and silhouettes, not icons.
Write or design the code/text layer intentionally. The copy-pasted pseudo-code and markdown artifacts read as filler and undercut the craft of the renders.
Introduce light and depth contrast. Every frame sits at the same flat blue value, so add a tonal arc or a single break in the palette to give the film a climax.

tells: The custom modular display type mixes Latin and katakana forms built from the same geometric parts ('TOKYO' resolving out of fragments). This is a real typographic idea.
The palette is unusual and deliberate (coral, cyan, chartreuse, violet on near-black) and holds across very different frames.

The frames are dense and layered: pixel matrices, scanline bands, framed type grids, diagonal bars. The composition changes radically from frame to frame, which implies varied choreography: assembly, scan, rotation, decay.
There is real texture: print-like grain, dot screens and misregistration rather than clean vector.
gaps: Anchor the system to an emotional or narrative beat. It is a superb type-and-glitch system, but C carries human presence and story.
Give the piece one held, quiet image. Every frame is at maximum density, and C's restraint (the glowing chip, the red sun) is what makes its peaks land.
Push the light: add one moment of photographic or volumetric light so the graphic world gets depth beyond flat layers.

tells: The idea is specific: the title sequence fuses early PC hardware with human silhouettes, scan-glitch and heat, and it pays off in the literal 'catch fire' red-sun end card.
It has real light and material: a macro chip glowing in a dish, horizontal light streaks, a burning orb, and film-like grain and bloom.
The palette is a single committed red/magenta whose value shifts from hot pink to deep ember across the sequence, giving it an arc.

The typography has a point of view: a restrained classical serif for credits set against a tracked, chunky, bitmap-adjacent title with a block glyph. The contrast between human and machine is the concept in type form.
Every frame works as a poster, and the frames vary in scale (macro, figure, abstract field) with clear choreography.
gaps: The credit serif placement is conventional (lower-centre). Integrating the names into the glitch/scan layer would push typography to a 10.
The middle frames (sticky-note squares) are briefly more diagrammatic than the rest; keep every beat as tactile as the chip and the orb.
There is little to fix. Minor: one more unexpected scale jump would add surprise before the end card.

tells: The typography is the idea: Latin and katakana-like letterforms are broken into modular strokes and dot-matrix fragments, then reassembled as 'TOKYO'. That is a custom, systematic typographic language, not a default face

The sequence implies choreography: glyphs scatter, rotate, resolve into pixels and then lock into the title
gaps: Light and texture are flat. Some print grain shows, but nothing physical gives it the material depth of A
Neon-Tokyo glitch typography is a crowded space. The concept needs a sharper hook beyond 'the city as a type system'
The final frame gets close to visual noise. A clearer hierarchy at the payoff would make the poster frame land

defects: The black reveal frame is almost empty: six grey tile fragments sit in the top strip with nothing below them. That's dead air with no compositional tension.
The opening staff shot holds for 4.0s, and in the pairs the tiles barely move across 1/6s. It reads as a slow scatter, not a played score.
During assembly, tiles appear as semi-transparent ghosts and diagonal triangle shards (pair row 2). They read as interpolation leftovers, not designed transitional states.
The red striped rule under the final wordmark is faint and shimmers against the grain, and is close to moiré at 100%.
The type system is spread too thin: tile display, condensed grotesk, wide grotesk, monospaced captions and outline numerals, with the vertical sidebar grotesk set very small.
The grain is a uniform overlay. There's no light, depth or falloff on the tiles, so they read as flat vector squares.
The orange date shot is static repetition (outline/solid/outline 14—29) with stray small squares in the corner that read as leftovers.
gaps: Motion has no weight or physical spacing. Tiles pop, fade or slide linearly instead of landing with anticipation, overshoot and settle on the notes. The concept (note tiles on a D–D octave staff building the wordmark) needs each tile to strike on its pitch and beat like a played instrument, with staggered overlap and follow-through.

Pacing and dead air: the 4s opening hold and the near-empty black frame drop the energy. The cut-in to the date card and the black field should be built from tile transitions, not hard swaps, keeping shots near 1.5s with the build peaking at about 70% of the runtime.

The sound is a thin, synthetic plucked arpeggio with reverb tails and repetitive clicks: few partials, little low-end weight and no designed foley for tiles snapping into letters. Pitch rows should map audibly to tile positions, and the final lock-up needs a real resolving hit and tail, not a decaying pad.
